title: Dictation Accuracy & Speed Benchmark | October 2026
summary: Our October 2026 benchmark tests 7 tools across 10 languages on accuracy and speed.
body_markdown:
Dictation accuracy claims rarely match what you experience in practice. A tool advertised at 95% accuracy still has you stopping to fix things constantly, because word error rate doesn't count the comma that changes your sentence's meaning or the capital letter that got dropped. We ran a different test across 7 tools and 10 languages, scoring only the outputs that needed no corrections at all. Willow Voice led all 10 languages in results that expose how misleading published accuracy figures can be.


**Willow Voice is the most accurate dictation software in this September 2026 benchmark, scoring 95% zero-edit rate in English and leading all 10 languages tested.** Across seven tools measured on zero-edit rate (the share of dictations that need no correction before use), Willow Voice scored between 85% and 95% depending on language. The next-closest competitor, Wispr Flow, scored between 80% and 90%. Apple Dictation, the built-in baseline, scored 35% to 48%. Results are from internal benchmark testing conducted in September 2026 across 10 languages and four passage types. Willow Voice also recorded the lowest latency in a separate five-tool speed benchmark: ~200ms on average-length dictations versus 900ms for Wispr Flow.

## Why Word Error Rate Misleads Desktop Dictation Users


Word Error Rate counts substitutions, deletions, and insertions, then divides by the total words in the reference transcript. A tool that gets 95% of words right scores a 5% WER, which sounds close to perfect. In a 200-word email, that still leaves 10 words wrong.


That arithmetic alone should give any knowledge worker pause. But WER has a second, less obvious problem: before scoring, most implementations strip punctuation and formatting. A missed comma, a broken paragraph, a dropped capital at the start of a sentence, none of those count as errors. As[Speechmatics notes](https://www.speechmatics.com/company/articles-and-news/the-problem-with-word-error-rate-wer) , WER was designed for research contexts measuring raw phoneme-to-word conversion, not for assessing whether a real user can send a message without touching their keyboard.


The result is a metric that flatters tools that fail in practice. A tool can score a respectable WER while still requiring you to stop, re-read, and correct formatting on every single dictation. Reviews of the[best AI speech to text tools](https://willowvoice.com/blog/best-ai-speech-to-text-tools) rarely surface this distinction. For someone clearing an inbox or filing a clinical note, those interruptions compound across dozens of messages a day. Rankings of the[best professional voice dictation software](https://willowvoice.com/blog/best-voice-dictation-software-mac-windows) confirm this pattern across tools. The corrections are small, but they are never free.


### Why Zero-Edit Rate Measures What Actually Matters


A more useful signal is whether the output is ready to send without any edits at all. Zero-edit rate captures exactly that: the share of dictations where the transcript required no correction before use. It accounts for punctuation, capitalization, formatting, and word choice simultaneously, because any one of those failures disqualifies the result.


That framing moves the question from "how many words did the tool get right?" to "how often can you trust the output completely?" For desktop dictation users, that distinction is the difference between a tool that saves time and one that just moves the correction work around.


## What Zero-Edit Rate Measures and Why It Is a Better Benchmark for Dictation


WER is a per-word score. Zero-edit rate is a per-output score.


WER is a per-word score. Zero-edit rate is a per-output score. A tool can mishandle punctuation on every dictation and never register a single WER penalty, because most WER implementations strip punctuation before scoring. Apple's own ML research on[humanizing WER for transcript readability](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/humanizing-wer) found that capitalization and punctuation errors are systematically excluded from standard WER scoring despite directly harming readability. Zero-edit rate catches that failure immediately: a missing comma that changes a sentence's meaning is a failed output regardless of how many words were technically correct.


The distinction matters most at the margins.


### Where WER Goes Silent


A 5% WER on a 100-word Slack message means roughly five words to fix, taking about 15 seconds. Across 30 messages a day, that adds up to seven minutes of correction time that never appears in a WER headline. Zero-edit rate makes it visible: if a tool produces a clean output only 60% of the time, you are editing 12 messages every day.


For professionals whose output is measured in communication volume, that correction loop is not a minor inconvenience. It is a context switch. You read back, locate the error, fix it, recheck, then return to whatever you were doing before you spoke. Each interruption costs more than the seconds it takes.


Zero-edit rate maps directly to that experience:


-


A score of 95% means 1 in 20 outputs needs a fix, close enough to invisible that dictation genuinely replaces typing.


-


A score of 85% means 1 in 6 outputs needs a fix, frequent enough to create a persistent secondary editing task that erodes the speed gain dictation was supposed to deliver.


Those numbers translate immediately into workflow terms that WER cannot reach. A comparison of[AI dictation tools](https://willowvoice.com/blog/best-ai-powered-dictation-tools) shows how widely zero-edit rates vary across products.


## Benchmark Methodology: Passages, Tools, and Conditions Tested


Four passage types formed the benchmark: a business email, technical software documentation with variable names and function references, a medical case summary with clinical terminology, and a Slack-style conversational exchange, each between 150 and 200 words.


Testing covered 10 languages: English, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Russian, French, Mandarin, Hindi, Japanese, and Korean, across seven tools: Apple Dictation, OpenAI, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, ElevenLabs, Wispr Flow, and Willow Voice. Superwhisper was excluded because its macOS-only distribution made consistent testing across all 10 languages impractical; a dedicated comparison is covered separately.


### Recording Conditions


All sessions used a USB headset with a close-talk microphone in a quiet room with no background noise. Each tool received a minimum of three hours of testing across multiple sessions and days.


### How Zero-Edit Rate Was Scored


A pass required no correction before use: no word substitutions, punctuation fixes, or formatting changes. A single required edit counted as a failed output. Two reviewers scored each transcript independently, with disagreements settled by a third review.

## Benchmark Results by Language


The sections below break down the September 2026 zero-edit rate findings for each language, with a spot for your benchmark graphic.


### English


Willow Voice scored 95% in English, leading all seven tools. Apple Dictation sits at 48%, making correction the default behavior on most outputs. Wispr Flow reached 90%, but the 5-point gap produces roughly 2 extra corrections per 40 daily dictations.


## Non-English Accuracy: Where Gaps Between Tools Widen


Non-English accuracy gaps are not random. Training data thins out, phoneme sets shift, and script complexity introduces recognition challenges with no Latin-alphabet equivalent. Those factors compound in predictable ways across the languages tested.


### Spanish


Willow Voice reaches 94% zero-edit rate in Spanish, close to its English result. Wispr Flow follows at 87%, a seven-point gap. Spanish tracks closely with English difficulty across most tools in this benchmark.


### Portuguese


Willow Voice scores 94% in Portuguese, matching its Spanish result. Wispr Flow drops further here, to 85%, a nine-point gap. Portuguese performs within a few points of English for most tools tested.


### Italian


Willow Voice posts 93% in Italian against Wispr Flow's 89%, a four-point gap, one of the tightest margins in the benchmark. Italian sits near English in overall difficulty for every tool tested.


### Russian


Russian word forms change based on grammatical case, and a model that guesses the wrong inflection produces an incorrect output even when the root word is recognized. Wispr Flow drops to 82% while Willow Voice holds at 93%, an 11-point gap, the largest between those two tools anywhere in the benchmark. The gap here traces to morphology rather than script.


### French


Willow Voice leads French at 92%, with Wispr Flow at 86%. OpenAI posts an 86% outlier in French, well above its results in other languages, pointing to denser training data for this language rather than a broader architecture edge. Silent letters and liaison rules create mismatches between how French sounds and how it must be written.


### Mandarin


Willow Voice scores 91% in Mandarin, with Wispr Flow trailing at 82%, a nine-point gap. Logographic script adds recognition and formatting challenges that most tools still struggle to close.


### Hindi


Willow Voice reaches 90% in Hindi against Wispr Flow's 85%, a five-point gap. Hindi scores fall below the Romance language group but ahead of the logographic languages tested.


### Japanese


Willow Voice posts 88% in Japanese, its second-lowest score in the benchmark, with Wispr Flow at 81%. AssemblyAI stands out here at 83%, outperforming every tool except Willow Voice, which points to targeted investment in Japanese recognition. Logographic script and dense morphology keep scores below the Romance language group for every tool tested.


### Korean


Korean produces the lowest scores of any language tested across every tool. Willow Voice leads at 85%, with Wispr Flow at 80%, a five-point gap. Logographic influence combined with complex morphology makes Korean the hardest language in this benchmark for every tool measured.


## Factors That Drive Real-World Accuracy Below Benchmark Scores


Benchmark scores represent a ceiling, not a guarantee. Controlled testing uses clean audio and consistent microphones, while real dictation happens under none of those conditions. Seven variables account for most of the gap between published scores and what users actually experience:


-


Microphone quality and placement: affects accuracy by 10 to 15%. A close-talk USB headset feeds a clean signal, while a built-in laptop mic picks up keystroke noise and room echo.


-


Background noise is the biggest factor. Accuracy can fall 30 to 40% in a loud office, coffee shop, or room with a fan running compared to a quiet space.


-


Speaking pace: fast speech clips word boundaries, while slow speech with long pauses can confuse phrase segmentation.


-


Accent and dialect: benchmark passages use standard reference speech, so regional accents or non-native speaker patterns can push recognition outside a model's training data.


-


Specialized vocabulary: technical terms, proper nouns, and drug names sit outside general vocabulary. A model that has never heard a term guesses from phonetic neighbors, often wrongly.


-


Filler word behavior: some tools strip "um" and "uh," others transcribe them verbatim, and mismatched handling adds correction work.


-


Latency spikes: brief network congestion can cause a model to segment audio wrong, producing run-on phrases or dropped words.


A tool scoring 90% under controlled conditions may perform closer to 78 to 82% in a busy open office with a built-in microphone.


## Accuracy Thresholds for Professional Use Cases


The right accuracy threshold depends on what happens when the output is wrong.


General business communication needs a zero-edit rate above 80%. At that rate, most messages go through clean, and the rare fix still costs less time than typing the message would have.


[Voice dictation for technical documentation](https://willowvoice.com/blog/voice-dictation-technical-documentation) raises the bar: a misrecognized variable name or API endpoint looks plausible but is functionally wrong. For code review comments and architecture notes, anything below 88 to 90% means each output needs a review pass before anyone trusts it.


Clinical and legal work sit at the top. A wrong drug name in a SOAP note or a transposed term in a legal brief can survive casual proofreading, so a zero-edit rate below 90% is a liability source, not a time saver. Vocabulary recognition for terms like Metformin, furosemide, or Latin legal phrases matters as much as the headline score. We break down how clinical tools compare on this threshold in our[medical dictation software rankings by zero-edit rate](https://willowvoice.com/blog/medical-dictation-software-ranked) .

## Transcription Latency: How Fast Does Text Appear?


Latency is one of the hardest problems in voice dictation to solve. Accuracy determines whether you edit your output. Latency determines whether you wait for it. A voice-first experience saves time only when text appears as you speak. At 700ms or more, you can feel the pause before text arrives; around 200ms, the gap is much harder to notice. That difference matters when an engineer speaks a prompt to a coding agent, a sales rep drafts an email, or a clinician captures a note. As dictations get longer, delays can interrupt the next thought.


Our September 2026 latency benchmark compares five consumer dictation tools at three dictation lengths. It is a separate test from the zero-edit rate benchmark above, which also includes speech-to-text model providers. The figures below measure transcription latency, not the total time needed to speak or review a document. For a tool-by-tool ranking of the fastest dictation apps, see our[speech-to-text latency benchmark.](https://willowvoice.com/blog/speech-to-text-latency-benchmark)


### Short Dictations (1-10 seconds)


In our short-dictation test, transcription latency was 190ms for Willow Voice, 400ms for Wispr Flow, 480ms for Superwhisper, 550ms for Aqua Voice, and 900ms for Typeless.


For a short Slack reply, Willow Voice recorded 190ms in our test. The other tools ranged from 400ms to 900ms, roughly two to nearly five times Willow's result. Even a brief message can end with a noticeable pause when text takes 900ms to appear.


### Average Dictations (10-60 seconds)


This range covers emails, Slack threads, meeting notes, and code review comments. Willow Voice measured 200ms, while Wispr Flow came in at 900ms. That is more than double its short-dictation result of 400ms and 4.5 times Willow's figure. Aqua Voice measured 600ms and Superwhisper 700ms, with Typeless at 1,000ms or more.


### Long Dictations (5+ minutes)


In our long-dictation test, transcription latency was 230ms for Willow Voice, 700ms for Wispr Flow, 800ms for Aqua Voice, 900ms for Superwhisper, and 1,100ms+ for Typeless.


On dictations lasting five minutes or more, Willow Voice measured 230ms. The next-fastest result was Wispr Flow at 700ms. For a legal brief, clinical note, or technical document, the gap between speaking and seeing text matters throughout the writing session. Willow's stated latency ceiling is 250ms across these dictation lengths; the measured results in these three tiers range from 190ms to 230ms.


> **Latency across dictation lengths:** Willow Voice rose by 40ms from short to long dictations (190ms to 230ms). Wispr Flow rose by 300ms (400ms to 700ms), although its average-length result was higher at 900ms. Superwhisper rose by 420ms (480ms to 900ms). Willow's measured latency stayed within a 40ms range across these three tiers.


### Why Local Models Are Not the Answer


On-device dictation can be useful when an internet connection is unavailable or local processing is required. Its speed and output quality depend on the model and the hardware, so local processing alone does not tell you whether a transcript will capture names, remove filler words, or format an email for its destination. The useful comparison is how quickly text appears and how much work remains after it does.


Willow Voice's cloud mode pairs roughly 200ms latency in this benchmark with context-aware vocabulary, filler-word cleanup, and formatting. An engineer can speak a prompt into Cursor or Claude Code and see it arrive without a long processing pause. A sales rep can dictate an email that takes the destination and writing style into account. A clinician can speak a note with medical terms recognized, then review it before adding it to a patient record. Willow also offers an offline mode on Mac and iOS for work that requires local processing; the cloud-mode latency figures here should not be treated as offline-mode measurements.

## FAQ


### How does zero-edit rate differ from word error rate as a dictation accuracy benchmark?


Word error rate scores individual words and ignores punctuation, capitalization, and formatting entirely, so a tool can produce a comma-free, uncapitalized wall of text and still post a respectable WER. Zero-edit rate measures whether the full output is ready to send without any changes at all, making it a direct measure of whether dictation actually replaces typing or just moves the correction work to a different step.


### Wispr Flow vs. Willow Voice across non-English languages: which holds up better?


Willow Voice leads in every language tested, but the gap widens considerably in morphologically complex languages. In Russian, the spread reaches 11 percentage points (93% vs. 82%); in Korean and Mandarin, Wispr Flow drops to 80 to 82% while Willow holds at 85 to 91%. For teams working across multiple languages daily, that difference compounds into a meaningfully higher correction load on the non-English portion of their output.


### What zero-edit rate do I need for clinical or legal dictation to be genuinely safe to use?


Both clinical and legal work require a zero-edit rate above 90% before dictation delivers net productivity gains instead of liability exposure. Below that threshold, a wrong drug name, misheard dosage, or transposed legal term can survive a casual proofread; the correction overhead stops being a minor inconvenience and becomes a patient safety or professional risk. General business communication has a lower bar at 80%, where most outputs clear without edits and the occasional fix still costs less time than typing the whole message.


### How do microphone choice and background noise affect real-world dictation accuracy compared to benchmark scores?


Benchmark scores represent a ceiling measured under clean conditions. Background noise alone can drop accuracy 30 to 40% compared to a quiet environment, and a built-in laptop microphone typically underperforms a close-talk USB headset by 10 to 15%. A tool scoring 90% in controlled testing may perform closer to 78 to 82% in an open office with its built-in mic, which is why the passage type, recording environment, and hardware used in any most accurate dictation software benchmark matter as much as the headline number.


### Can Willow Voice handle technical documentation and medical terminology accurately enough for professional use?


Yes. Willow Voice scored 95% in English across all four passage types in this benchmark, including technical software documentation with variable names and medical case summaries with clinical terminology. Its context-aware engine reads the active application to adjust vocabulary expectations before transcription begins, and the Auto-Dictionary builds a personalized vocabulary from corrections over time, so terms like function references, drug names, and domain-specific jargon stop being failure points instead of requiring manual dictionary entry each session.
